nodes.body: The duty phone rattles on the nightstand at 04:40. It's the caretaker at Château Vaudren, which sits at the head of the Tarnoux terrace, and he's already breathing the word 'notifiable' before Ines Kollar can find the light switch. He's found a fresh mark on the vines—a canker she knows from photographs, never from standing in a row at dawn with the dew still on her boots. She asks him to repeat the location, then the variety, then whether he's touched anything. He hasn't. That's something.

Ines Kollar, district phytosanitary officer for the Tarnoux watershed, dresses in the dark and runs a sequence she's rehearsed for eleven years and never used. The valley is a patchwork of seventy-four growers, two co-operatives that share a crushing facility, and a single road that connects every terrace to the market towns below. Whatever she does in the next hour sets the shape of the next month for all of it. The growers will need to be told before the sun is fully up. Some of them will have already heard. She pulls on her field jacket, tests the GPS unit in her kit bag, and goes out to the cold car, already knowing the shape of the question she does not yet know how to answer: how far, and for how long.

choices.label: Go straight in and look at the vines.
Ask for the movement records before anything else.
Walk the boundary first and see how the place leaks.

nodes.body: The east-facing terrace at Vaudren at ten past six, the sun rising over the river mist and the vines still heavy with a harvest that was supposed to start this week. Nothing is being picked. Paul Rennick stands at the head of the row with his secateurs hanging uselessly from his belt loop and eleven vines showing the mark: a blistering at the graft union, discoloration spreading upward through the cordons, and a smell like wet cork. He tells her he noticed it three days ago and thought it was sun-scald. She doesn't know him well enough to know if that's true. The dew is burning off fast now and she's aware of the heat that will be on the terrace by nine o'clock, pushing volatiles into the air if there's anything airborne.

The domaine office is a narrow room under a hot, corrugated roof. The desk is an old door laid across two filing cabinets. Rennick has already got the spray diary out and it lies open. It shows fourteen days of entries in three different pens. One is a fine-nibbed fountain pen that is not his, recording a contractor on the terrace for two days of leaf-plucking. The contractor left before the weekend. The diary also records a delivery of young vines from a nursery in the next valley three weeks ago. This is the most ordinary thing in the world and now the most alarming. Ines photographs every page with her phone before the light shifts because she has learned that paper changes when people have time to think about what it says.

choices.label: Start with the people inside the line.

nodes.body: She walks the boundary in the half-dark before the heat builds. She checks the roadside gate that opens onto the D4. She checks the tractor turning circle where the spray tankers fill up, and the gap where an old stone wall was taken down two winters ago to run a drainage pipe. She also checks a public footpath that runs within thirty metres of the affected terrace. The footpath is on the tourism board's map, dotted and cheerful, and it cuts through four more vineyards before it reaches the river. At the turning circle she finds a deep rut made by a heavy vehicle, still wet with dew caught in the tread marks. She photographs it before she realizes she is treating it as evidence. That means she has already decided this is an outbreak, not just a single odd canker.

choices.label: Start with the people inside the line.

nodes.body: The containment zone is three kilometres across, drawn on a laminated vineyard map with a wax pencil. In this valley, that circle means thirty-one growers, two of them across the river Tarnoux with no bridge inside the line. The map is ten years old and does not show the new plantings on the south slope, which means she is already working from a flawed record in ways that will matter. Through the window of the domaine office she can see the first pickers arriving on bicycles for a harvest that now cannot happen. She has to go out and tell them before they enter the rows. She does it in French and then again in the patois the older ones use because she needs them to grasp not just the order but the gravity of it. One woman sets her bicycle against the gatepost and simply waits, as though waiting will reverse the morning.

choices.label: Set up in the village hall.

nodes.body: The surveillance zone extends to ten kilometres. It takes in the co-op crusher at Saint-Marc, the bottling plant road at Pont-Bernard, the nursery that shipped the young vines, and most of the growers who will be angry about it by lunchtime. The zone also captures two vineyards that sell fully to a merchant in Beaune. His contracts have penalty clauses for non-delivery, and he will be on the phone to the authorities within the hour. Ines is drawing a line around people's entire annual income, and she knows it. There is no version of this morning where the line does not feel random to everyone on the wrong side of it. One of the growers inside the surveillance zone is her own cousin, Thierry. She last saw him at a wedding and now she has to call him.

choices.label: Set up in the village hall.

nodes.body: Road closures: four lanes and a farm track that runs along the riverbank. None of them can be shut without cutting somebody off from a pharmacy, a school bus stop, or the only road to the doctor in Verrière. The gendarmerie liaison is a sergeant named Lefèvre whom she has dealt with twice on livestock cases. He wants a list in twenty minutes and he wants to know if she even has the legal power to close the D4. She does, technically, under the 2014 plant health order, but she has never used it and neither has anyone in his office. He is asking her to be certain before he puts a barrier across a road his own children take to school. She is not certain, not about any of it, but the alternative is traffic moving through the containment zone all morning carrying vineyard soil on its tyres.

choices.label: Set up in the village hall.

nodes.body: She considers the people rather than the vines: who lives inside the line, who works across it tending other people's terraces, which of them depend on the harvest for day wages that will stop today, and how many of them will hear this first from a neighbour before she can reach them with the official version. The valley has seventy-four growers but only about half of them own the land. The rest are tenants, share-croppers, or families who work a few rows under contract to a larger domaine. A standstill hits them first and hardest, and they are the ones the official leaflets always reach last because the system records land ownership, not labour. She starts a list of names on the back of her field notebook and knows at once it is not complete. She has been in this district five years and there are still people here who will not appear on any register she can access. They will appear on the phone tree instead.

The first page of the movement ledger is drawn by hand in the Tarnoux village hall at nine at night. The columns are: date, domaine, material moved, quantity, reason, decision, and signature. She adds a column herself, drawing the line with a ruler from the caretaker's drawer, for what she was told. No regulation asks for that column. She creates it because she knows, from eleven years of reading other people's outbreak diaries, that the official columns never capture the thing that later turns out to have mattered. The room smells of the coffee urn and someone's wet coat. Outside the open window a dog barks at something in the vineyard dark.

choices.label: Open the door to the queue.

nodes.body: The phone tree: seventy-four growers, two people calling—herself and a district assistant named Martin who she's pulled in from the next valley—and the awkward truth that the fastest route through the watershed is gossip. She's choosing to use it. She drafts the script carefully, keeping the language flat, 'suspected detection' rather than 'outbreak,' 'voluntary restriction' rather than 'standstill,' and the third person she calls, a grower named Madame Faucher on the upper terrace, already knows. She knows because her son saw the wax pencil marks on the map through the domaine office window and texted her. By the time Ines reaches the sixth call, the valley is already ahead of her.

choices.label: Deal with the harvested fruit first.

nodes.body: The hall itself contains trestle tables and a hot water urn, a stack of plastic chairs pushed against the far wall, and a caretaker named Monsieur Beck. He unlocked it without being asked and is now setting the tables into rows as if for a village fête. It becomes a control centre in the time it takes to move the badminton nets and plug in an extension lead. Beck brings her a cup of coffee and a plate of biscuits and asks no questions. She watches him straighten the chairs and realizes he is treating this the way he treated the flood in '08, as something the valley copes with by opening the hall. This is probably the right instinct, even if the science says otherwise.

The mechanical harvester has already run its route this vintage, three domaines deep, before anybody thought to stop it. Its driver now sits in a lay-by on the D4 with the machine idling, waiting to be told what he is. He is a contractor from outside the valley who works the harvest circuit every year from here down to the Rhône. The harvester's picking head is carrying leaf debris, soil, and possibly infection from three different vineyards. He asks, quite fairly, whether he is allowed to wash the machine and go home. She does not yet know whether the blight is mechanically transmissible, but she knows the harvester cannot leave the valley until she does.

The sign: a new one, still with the protective film on the plastic, cable-tied to the gatepost at the valley mouth by Sergeant Lefèvre's youngest constable. It reads 'ZONE RÉGLEMENTÉE – PHYLLOXERA-LIKE ORGANISM SUSPECTED' in a font that somebody at the préfecture chose from a drop-down menu, and it is somehow the most real thing that has happened all day. Cars slow down to read it. A delivery van driver photographs it with his phone. The laminated plastic catches the morning light and shines like a thing that has always been there, which is exactly what it's supposed to do and exactly what makes it unnerving. She stands beside it for a full minute, in the quiet of the closed road, before her phone rings again.

choices.label: Take the call from the regional director.

nodes.body: A queue forms at the hall door by half seven, twenty deep, carrying paperwork and phones. In two cases, people are holding actual vine samples in plastic bags which nobody asked them to bring. Most of them are holding spray diaries, delivery dockets, or hastily written lists of people who have been on their land in the last fourteen days. None of it is the right paperwork because the right paperwork does not exist yet. A man named Gilles from the lower terraces has brought his entire vintage log going back to 2011, leather-bound, and is leafing through it while he waits like a man looking up a scripture. The queue smells of coffee, woodsmoke from the morning baker's oven, and the particular anxiety of people who have been told to wait and do not yet know what for. She opens the door.

choices.label: Go up to the old-vine parcel at Montjoie.
Go to the nursery block at Les Sources.
Order the harvested grapes destroyed and stop there.

nodes.body: Vaudren is producing four tonnes a day of fruit that can go nowhere: the grape bins are full, the next picking was supposed to start in six hours, and the only lawful destination for harvested fruit in a containment zone is destruction. Rennick is standing in the cold room with the lights off because he can't bear to look at the bins. The grapes are Chardonnay, perfectly ripe, the sugars tested and the picking date chosen three months ago, and the economics of this one harvest represent his entire operating loan for the year. He asks her, standing in the dark with his arms crossed, whether there's any possibility of a derogation for wine that's already fermented. She has to tell him that the crushed berries haven't even begun their maceration yet and that processing of any kind inside the zone requires a licence she hasn't even designed. The silence in the cold room is colder than the air.

choices.label: Go to the nursery block at Les Sources.
Go to the smallholding at La Garenne.

nodes.body: The team briefing: two phytosanitary inspectors seconded from the adjoining regions, one of whom, a woman named Karine from the Savoie office, has done this before in the Swiss canton of Vaud and is quietly certain everything here is at least ten days too late. She's looking at the map on the wall with the expression of someone doing arithmetic in her head. Her quiet certainty is the most reassuring and the most alarming thing in the room. She asks Ines, in front of everyone, whether the lab samples went to Colmar or Lyon, because the turnaround time differs by thirty-six hours. Ines doesn't know yet—she hasn't dispatched the samples—and the silence that follows that admission rearranges something in the hierarchy of the room.

choices.label: Go to the smallholding at La Garenne.
Stay with the queue and let the day go.

nodes.body: The first licence she refuses, to a grower named Benoît who wants to move two hundred kilos of Pinot Noir grapes he's already sold to a négociant in a neighbouring commune. The contract is signed, the price agreed, the picking bins are sitting on his trailer, and he's not wrong: the sale won't survive the delay, the négociant will source from elsewhere, and he'll lose not just this vintage but probably the contract for next year too. He's standing in the hall with the bill of sale in his hand, creased from his pocket, and he's asking her to look at the economics of it, just the economics. She looks. The economics are real and they are not a factor she's authorised to consider. She writes 'REFUSED – CONTAINMENT DIRECTIVE' in the ledger and he watches her do it, and the look on his face is the first time today she's felt personally responsible for something that is actually the blight's fault.

choices.label: Go to the smallholding at La Garenne.

nodes.body: Solveig Bett, regional director, on a bad line from a car on the autoroute, wanting the zone smaller and the language calmer and the numbers by ten o'clock. She's already had a call from the préfet, who's had a call from the mayor's office, who's had a call from the tourism board, and everyone wants the same thing: containment without the appearance of containment, a standstill that doesn't alarm anyone, a crisis that ends before the weekend. Bett uses the word 'proportionate' three times in ninety seconds. Ines, standing in the hall lobby with the phone pressed to her ear, explains that the suspected organism is vascular, not insect-borne, which means it could have been moving through graft unions for weeks before anyone saw a mark, which means the surveillance zone at ten kilometres is conservative, not proportionate, and 'proportionate' is the word you use when you've already decided what you're willing to lose. The line goes quiet. 'Ten o'clock,' Bett says, and hangs up.

Montjoie, a parcel of old-vine Grenache on the south-facing slope above Vaudren: low-trained goblet bush vines, gnarled and beautiful, belonging to the Fauvet family who were planning to start picking next week for the co-operative. The Fauvets are gathering in the yard when she arrives, three generations, already knowing something is wrong because nobody from the district office drives up the Montjoie track at nine in the morning on a harvest week unless something is very wrong. The oldest Fauvet, a woman named Céline who planted some of these vines herself in 1973, asks whether they have to pull anything. Ines hasn't said anything about pulling yet but Céline has been through the 2003 heatwave and the 1991 freeze and she knows what containment looks like when it reaches old vines. The question hangs in the morning air between them with the smell of ripening Grenache.

choices.label: Look at the canopy problem on the slope.
Do the arithmetic at the nursery.
Decide what happens to the harvested grapes.

nodes.body: Les Sources is a nursery block run on a tight graft-and-ship schedule by Mahesh Ubaid. Stopping movement does not stop growth. The rootlings are in pots and the grafted vines are pushing callus. The whole operation runs on a four-week growing cycle. This leaves about six days of slack in the benches. Ubaid walks her through the tunnel houses with a clipboard. He shows her the order book, the delivery schedule, and the exact date when the first finished grafts will outgrow their pots. The date is nine days from now. He is polite, methodical, and terrified. His entire business model is moving plant material across biosecurity boundaries. A standstill order is an existential threat. She tells him she will do what she can. He thanks her and goes back to his clipboard. She can see him already recalculating the sums of a business that might not survive the month.

choices.label: Do the arithmetic at the nursery.
Decide what happens to the harvested grapes.
Sort out waste plant material collection.
Get the paperwork right before anything moves.

nodes.body: The Brayne table-grape trellises, four hectares of trellised fruit grown for the fresh market, bought in as young vines from six different nurseries over the last three years. The provenance trail is either a biosecurity nightmare or the best available map of where the blight has already come from, and Ines can't yet tell which. The grower, a young woman named Lucie Brayne who took over from her father last year, is walking her down the rows explaining the planting dates with the precision of someone who already knows this information is going to matter. Her trellises are immaculate, her spray records are digital, and the two cankers her own scout found this morning are in vines that came from a nursery in the Rhône valley that has since gone out of business. The records stop there. The trail, where it matters most, simply ends.

choices.label: Decide what happens to the harvested grapes.
Sort out waste plant material collection.
Go and see the diseased Syrah vine.

nodes.body: La Garenne: four rows of table grapes, a polytunnel of tomatoes, and a patch of old hybrid vines belonging to Otto Sarre. He did not know he was a grower under the 2014 order until this morning. He's a retired schoolteacher who makes his own wine for family weddings and sells a little honey at the market. He has never registered with the district office because nobody ever told him he needed to. She finds him in the polytunnel, tying up tomatoes. When she explains the situation, he listens carefully, nods, and then asks a fair question. He wants to know if the order applies to him at all since his vines aren't Vitis vinifera. In his words, they are 'more root than anything.' It's a good question. The order doesn't distinguish. She tells him it applies anyway. The look he gives her—puzzled, not angry—makes her feel like she's enforcing a rule designed for someone else's valley.

choices.label: Sort out waste plant material collection.
Go and see the diseased Syrah vine.
Deal with the hybrid vines at La Garenne.

nodes.body: She checks the shared water source. It is a header tank on the parish line. Three estates have drawn from it since before any of them signed up with the water board. It is a concrete tank, likely built in the 1960s. It is fed by a spring and piped down the slope. The network of black plastic pipes was laid by the growers themselves over decades. Nobody knows exactly where the pipes run. Nobody has a diagram. If the blight is water-borne via root contact, this single tank could link vines that are miles apart on the map. She takes photos of the tank, the pipe joins, and the slime line where the water level has dropped in the summer heat. She knows she is writing down a shared resource no rule ever planned for. No one at the ministry ever dreamed a valley would water itself by friendly deal since before the ministry was born.

choices.label: Go and see the diseased Syrah vine.
Deal with the hybrid vines at La Garenne.
Talk to the grape-bin lorry driver.
Let the valley tell you what it knows.

nodes.body: The footpath runs the length of the valley next to the river. It is marked with yellow paint on the oak trees. It is popular with weekend walkers from Verrière. It is also very hard to close by law. It is listed on the county's rights-of-way register under a 1983 name that nobody in the legal office can quickly find. The path runs within thirty metres of the sick terrace at Vaudren. It cuts through two other vineyards. It passes the spring-fed water tank. Every Saturday morning, even now, walkers with poles and backpacks use it. Their boots carry valley soil from one end of the water basin to the other. The question is not if the path is a risk. It is if anyone has the power to shut something older than the vines themselves. She will need the mayor, a short-term order, and a public notice. It will show up in the local paper and quickly cause a letter from the hiking club. They have a lawyer.

choices.label: Deal with the hybrid vines at La Garenne.
Talk to the grape-bin lorry driver.
Look at the canopy problem on the slope.

nodes.body: A contractor's narrow tractor, the kind that straddles the rows, which has worked on nine domaines in twelve days doing leaf-plucking and green-harvest thinning and is currently parked, unwashed, in a shed at the tenth. The contractor, a man named Ferrand, is defensive and then helpful and then frightened, because he understands exactly what it means that she's photographing his machine. The tractor's chassis is carrying soil from every vineyard it visited, the wheels are caked with dried mud that's still shedding clods onto the shed floor, and the leaf-plucking head has fragments of green tissue caught in the rollers that could have come from anywhere. He offers to wash it. She tells him not to touch it until she's taken samples. They both stand looking at the machine for a long moment, this ordinary piece of equipment that has become a vector, while Ferrand's phone buzzes in his pocket with the next job he won't be able to do.

choices.label: Talk to the grape-bin lorry driver.
Look at the canopy problem on the slope.
Do the arithmetic at the nursery.

nodes.body: The canopy at Montjoie is in full leaf and overdue for trimming, and the grower who normally does it—a contractor with a tractor-mounted trimmer—is on the far side of the closed lane and can't legally reach the parcel. The vines will carry too much leaf mass into the hottest week of the month, transpiration will spike, and the old Grenache, which has survived heatwaves before, will start to suffer drought stress inside ten days if the canopy isn't managed. The Fauvets can do some of it by hand but they're short-staffed because their usual pickers can't enter the zone, and Céline Fauvet is seventy-one and can only work a row for so long before the heat gets her. It's not the blight itself that will damage these vines; it's the standstill. She knows this, and there's no column in the ledger for secondary harm.

choices.label: Sleep four hours at the hall and carry on.
Go and confirm the second case yourself.
Drive up to the slope before the light goes.
Leave the slope to sort its own pruning.

nodes.body: Les Sources is filling: new grafts coming through from the propagation house behind mature vines that can't leave, and Ubaid is doing arithmetic on a feed bag that ends in a number of days rather than a plan. He's drawn a grid in felt-tip on the white plastic: the bench numbers down the side, the dates across the top, and a diagonal line representing the moment when each batch outgrows its pot and must either be shipped or dumped. The first batch hits that line in nine days. He's not asking her for permission; he's showing her the arithmetic because he needs someone official to see it before it becomes a crisis. She photographs the feed bag, then realises the felt-tip grid is his real record—more accurate than anything on his computer—and asks if she can take that too. He hesitates, then hands it over. 'It's going to end up in a report, isn't it,' he says. It's not a question.

choices.label: Go and confirm the second case yourself.
Drive up to the slope before the light goes.
Go down to the boundary and see the watchers.
Hold the line on the nursery and move nothing.

nodes.body: Nine domaines now have bins of harvested grapes in cold storage. Some of the fruit has already begun to oxidise. A proposal has come from the co-operative at Saint-Marc to take the grapes out of the zone under seal for immediate crushing. The plan is sensible. It involves sealed lorries, dedicated tanks, and traceable lot numbers. But it is also the exact way to spread anything in the juice or skins to a shared facility that processes fruit from many valleys. She cannot authorise it without a risk assessment that nobody has written. She cannot refuse it without being seen to choose destruction over a practical fix. The co-op director is on the phone, polite and insistent. He points out that a sealed container is the very definition of biosecurity. She tells him she'll get back to him within the hour. The hour has already been gone for forty minutes.

choices.label: Drive up to the slope before the light goes.
Go down to the boundary and see the watchers.
Take the morning calls from the other valleys.

nodes.body: Waste plant material collection has stopped at the zone boundary and there are already piles of prunings, pulled weeds, and rejected fruit that need collecting, in August, in the heat. The usual contractor who does the valley's green-waste run operates a shredder truck that isn't allowed to cross the line, and the alternative—stacking the waste on site—creates a pest and disease reservoir exactly where nobody wants one. Two growers have already called to ask, with varying degrees of politeness, whether she intends to let the waste rot and breed something worse. She doesn't. She also doesn't have a solution, and the man at the waste authority in Verrière who might authorise a derogation is on holiday until Monday. Monday is five days away, and the heat is not going to stop for the weekend.

choices.label: Go down to the boundary and see the watchers.
Take the morning calls from the other valleys.

nodes.body: A diseased Syrah vine at Brayne is one of the old block. It shows classic leaf scorch and a canker at the graft that has almost certainly been there since last season. Lucie Brayne found it during her own walk-through and called it in immediately. It needs a proper inspection by someone with a knife, a magnifier, and the authority to take tissue samples. Every inspector in the valley is doing visits to holdings that might be infected, rather than examining the one that definitely is. The Syrah sits there in its row, showing symptoms and patient, while the morning heats up and the sample transport window closes. It is the most clearly important job of the day and she cannot get to it. The day is structured around prevention, not diagnosis. This is the opposite of what the field manual says and exactly what happens when a desk in a ministry writes a protocol for a valley it has never visited.

choices.label: Take the morning calls from the other valleys.
Sit down with the ledger and read it back.

nodes.body: The La Garenne hybrid vines, which are not a susceptible Vitis vinifera variety—they're a French-American hybrid probably planted in the 1980s—and belong to Otto Sarre, who now cannot legally enter his own polytunnel because the path from his house crosses the containment line. The vines themselves are in good health and showing no marks, and Sarre is phoning her from his kitchen, which is fifty metres from his vines but on the wrong side of an invisible boundary drawn on a map he's never seen. He's polite about it, and patient, and he simply wants to know how he's supposed to water his tomatoes. She realises, listening to his question, that she's drawn a line through the middle of a man's daily life and the guidance document has no section on polytunnels. She tells him she'll find a way. He thanks her and hangs up, and the phone in her hand is heavier than it was.

choices.label: Sit down with the ledger and read it back.
Sleep four hours at the hall and carry on.

nodes.body: A bin lorry driver is at the roadblock on the D4. He has eleven drops booked for the morning, a refrigerated load of empty bins that need to go back to their growers, and a tachograph that will not forgive an argument. He has been sitting at the barrier for forty minutes with the engine off to save fuel. When Ines arrives, he gets out of the cab with the delivery schedule in his hand. He looks like a man who has been given an order by his dispatcher and cannot understand why a laminated sign is stopping him. She explains the containment order. He asks if he can at least drop the empty bins and come straight back out. She has to say no. The look on his face is not anger, exactly. It's the slow recognition that his day's work has just been made impossible by a thing growing on a vine he has never seen. He gets back in his cab and calls his dispatcher. She can hear the dispatcher's voice through the window, loud and incredulous, asking what kind of disease stops a lorry from dropping off empty plastic.

choices.label: Sit down with the ledger and read it back.
Sleep four hours at the hall and carry on.
Go and confirm the second case yourself.
Follow the tractor and nothing else.

nodes.body: Day four: the hall smells of wet coats and coffee brewed too strong, the ledger is on its ninth page and the ink has started to smudge where people have leaned over it. Nobody has been home for more than an hour since the call came in, and the team is running on the particular exhaustion that comes from making decisions that feel consequential and also provisional, because every answer she gives today might be revised by something found tomorrow. Martin has fallen asleep on a bench at the back of the hall with his clipboard on his chest. She lets him sleep. Outside, the morning sun is already hot on the road, and somewhere up on the terraces a vine is shedding enough inoculum to keep her here for another week.

Day four in the rows: the second confirmed case at Vaudren has been found by Karine from Savoie. She went looking for it exactly where she said it would be—three rows east of the first, in a vine from the same rootstock batch. She calls it in at eight in the morning, her voice level and professional. Ines can hear in the flatness of it that Karine did not want to be the one to confirm it. Being right about a second case means being right about the speed of the spread. Being right about the speed means the ten-kilometre surveillance zone was optimistic. Ines writes 'CONFIRMED – 2nd SITE' in the ledger next to the Vaudren entry. The pen feels different in her hand now, as though the book itself is getting heavier.

Day four on the slope: the Fauvet family have started trimming by hand what they would normally run the tractor through, working the rows with secateurs and a hand-saw and a quiet fury that Ines can feel from the track. Céline is on the third row, her son Alain on the fifth, and they are doing what the valley has always done when the machinery can't reach—working anyway, slowly, the old way, because the vines won't wait for a ministerial decision. The canopy is getting ahead of them. Ines can see, even from the track, that they'll lose two rows to the heat before they finish, and she can also see that they know this and are trimming anyway because stopping would be worse. Nobody speaks to her when she arrives. They nod, and keep cutting, and the sound of the secateurs is the only conversation they're willing to have.

Day four at the boundary: two lay-bys on the D4 have become informal viewing points for people who want to look at the zone signs and take photographs. A car with Belgian plates is parked at the first lay-by. The driver is holding a phone out of the window. A man in walking gear is at the second, studying the laminated notice with the focus of someone memorising it. The signs themselves are still clean, still bright, still shining with that wrong-font authority. They have attracted exactly the kind of attention she hoped they would not. Sergeant Lefèvre has posted a constable at the main barrier but not at the lay-bys. The lay-bys are outside the zone, and the constables have other things to do. The photographs will appear online—probably are already online. The valley's name will be attached to a disease before the disease is even confirmed by the lab. She has seen this happen to other districts. Now it is happening here, to this sign, in this light, while she stands watching.

Day four in the office: three neighbouring valleys now want the Tarnoux numbers before their own morning calls. A vascular blight does not respect watershed boundaries. Every district officer for fifty kilometres is now drawing their own lines in their own notebooks. The calls are collegial, professional, and edged with the same question: has it reached us, are we next, did we miss something? She gives them what she can—confirmed sites, suspect varieties, the date of the first mark according to Rennick. She can hear them writing it down. She can hear the pause while they map it against their own terraces. One of them, a man named Delambre from the next valley east, tells her he has already started his own ledger, just in case. He does not mean it as a criticism. It lands like one anyway: the expectation that this will spread, that her containment is temporary, that his valley is next.

Day four on the phone: the first anonymous report of an illegal movement, and it names somebody. The voice on the line is male, older, and he gives a grower's name—Claude Perrin, a smallholder on the upper terrace. He says Perrin moved pruned wood off his property last night after dark using a tractor and trailer. The caller will not give his own name. She presses, gently, and he hangs up. She writes 'REPORTED – PERRIN – PRUNINGS – NIGHT MOVE' in the ledger's margin because she does not yet know what to do with anonymous information. The report might be true, or it might be a grudge dressed up as civic duty. The Perrin family have been in the valley since before anyone can remember and have had a boundary dispute with their neighbour since 2012. She is going to have to investigate a rumour that might destroy a family or might save a valley. She will not know which until she knocks on Claude Perrin's door and asks him to account for his tractor movements in the dark.

Day four in the ledger: the column she added for what she was told is now the most interesting column in the book. It contains fragments—'wife saw markings 3 wks ago,' 'contractor Ferrand here 9 days,' 'neighbour uses same trellis wire'—that don't fit in any official category but are already, four days in, showing patterns the formal records miss. Karine reads the column over her shoulder and says nothing, which is the most significant acknowledgement the column has received. Ines closes the book and puts it in her bag, and for a moment she feels about the ledger the way she once felt about a field notebook during her first outbreak—that it's the only record that will outlast the meeting minutes, the press releases, and the final report. It won't be admissible. It might be right.

choices.label: Ask the question about wind and insects.

nodes.body: The Saint-Marc co-op delivery ledger for the last three crush days, thirty pages of carbon-copy dockets in a ring binder that smells of fermenting must. Half the entries are in a hand—spidery, abbreviated—that identifies growers by the name of a domaine owner who died in 2009, and nobody currently working at the co-op can reliably translate it. The ledger records deliveries by weight and lot number but doesn't record the vineyard of origin for fruit from mixed parcels, which is most of it, because the co-op was designed for vinification, not traceability. The cellar master, a young man named Hervé who has been in the job for three months, is standing beside her looking at the book like it's evidence against him personally. She asks him to walk her through a single delivery, from arrival to pressing. He can tell her the tonnage, the variety, and the tank it went into, but he can't tell her which rows the grapes came from. The information doesn't exist. The trail ends at the weighbridge.

The Pont-Bernard crusher consignment records, which are digital, complete, searchable by lot number, and cover only the fruit that actually arrived at the weighbridge. The system is the best in the district—invoiced, auditable, and entirely irrelevant, because it was built to track payments, not plant material. It tells her exactly how many tonnes of each variety crossed the scales on any given day, which is not the same as telling her which vineyards supplied them, because the crusher accepts fruit from brokers who aggregate deliveries from multiple small growers into single lots. The broker's paperwork, which is where the provenance trail lives, is in a filing cabinet in an office in Beaune and won't be accessible until someone drives there with a warrant or a very politely worded request. She phones the broker's office. The receptionist tells her the director is in a meeting and will call back. The meeting has been going on for four hours, which she takes as an answer.

The grafting technician did a round of six estates in two days. He carried bench grafts, binding tape, and a grafting knife. The knife moved from vine to vine without being cleaned between cuts. He keeps his diary in his head. No notebook, no phone app. Just a memory that is famous in the valley for being more reliable than written records. His name is Gaspard. He has been grafting in the Tarnoux watershed for thirty years. When she asks him to rebuild his movements, he closes his eyes. He recites the dates, the vineyard names, the rootstock types, and the exact rows he worked on. He does this without any pause. It is a great show, but it is also completely unverifiable. She writes it all down anyway. His memory is the only cross-domain trace for six different places right now. And if he is right, the graft union at Vaudren was cut less than a week before the first mark appeared. The timeline is starting to compress.

The pruning gang is five men and a trailer. They worked the Montjoie and upper-terrace plots in the last two weeks. Now they are on a different slope in a different valley. They are unreachable by phone. The gang leader's mobile has no signal in the Hautes-Côtes. They moved through the valley in a single week, working fast. Their tools were not washed between estates. Nobody asks a pruning gang to clean their secateurs between rows in a normal season. If the blight can spread on cutting blades, the lab in Colmar hasn't ruled it out yet. Then these five men carried it from one end of the watershed to the other without ever knowing. She needs to find them, talk to them, and trace their exact route. She needs to do this before they move on to the next job and the next valley. Martin is already driving up to the Hautes-Côtes. He has a list of the farms they had contracts for. His phone will be out of range within the hour.

choices.label: Look at the summer wine fair.

nodes.body: The mechanical harvester route is a list of gates opened in a set order. It covers three estates on the morning they declared the quarantine. The harvester driver is the man in the lay-by. His name is Jacques Leclerc. He keeps a log on a clipboard in the cab. It has the date, time, estate name, and variety. There is a column for notes. He writes things like 'row 14 skipped, bird damage.' His log is the best evidence in the valley. It records exactly where the machine stopped, turned, and moved between rows. If the blight is mechanical, Leclerc's clipboard is the closest thing Ines has to a disease map. She brings it back to the hall. She spreads the pages across two trestle tables and weights the corners with coffee cups. For the first time since the phone rang at 04:40, she feels like she is looking at something that tells a clear story. It is no longer just pieces of one.

choices.label: Look at the summer wine fair.
Work the paperwork that does not match.

nodes.body: A walker who posted photographs of the Vaudren terrace eight days ago, geotagged and dated, showing the vine rows in full leaf with the river in the background. The photographs are on a public hiking forum, captioned 'Tarnoux Valley – perfect morning light,' and they have been viewed four hundred times and liked by twelve people. The walker, whose username is 'randonneur_71,' has since walked four other valleys and posted photographs of each, and in every one his boots are caked with soil that has now travelled from the Tarnoux watershed to three different départements. The geotag on the Vaudren photograph places him exactly on the public footpath, thirty metres from the affected terrace, on a day when the first canker would almost certainly have been visible if he'd known what to look at. She can't prove he carried anything. She also can't prove he didn't. The hiking forum has no contact details, and randnonneur_71 hasn't posted since Sunday. She forwards the link to the préfecture's communications officer with a note that says only: 'This is the one the press will find first.'

choices.label: Look at the summer wine fair.
Work the paperwork that does not match.
Accept that the footpath cannot be closed.

nodes.body: The question nobody wants asked out loud: windblown rain splash, leafhoppers, and the mist that rolls up the valley from the river every evening, which would mean the lines on the map are decoration and the blight has been moving through the watershed for weeks by means the containment order was never designed to stop. The question is raised quietly by Karine, who has seen airborne spread in Switzerland and who asks it not in the main briefing but afterwards, at the coffee urn, with her back to the room. If it's airborne, she says, then the three-kilometre line is a political boundary, not a phytosanitary one, and everything Ines has done for four days has been about reassuring people who wanted to see a line drawn on a map. She's not saying this to be cruel. She's saying it because the lab needs to prioritise the transmission study and right now the lab doesn't know the question exists. Ines pours herself another coffee and stares at the wall, and for a long moment neither of them says anything else.

choices.label: Work the paperwork that does not match.
Keep writing down what people tell you.

nodes.body: The Saint-Marc co-op office, where the director, a woman named Madame Fournier, is helpful, frightened, and in possession of a second delivery log she has not mentioned. It's a spiral notebook, kept in her desk drawer, recording the informal deliveries that growers make outside the official weighbridge hours—a bucket of late-picked grapes, a few crates from an overlooked row, the kind of casual contributions that the valley has always treated as too small to document. She produces it when Ines asks specifically about the last week of July, and her hands are shaking slightly when she passes it across the desk. 'This isn't official,' she says, and Ines tells her it is now. The notebook adds seven domaines to the list of suppliers who delivered fruit to the crusher during the likely infection window, and one of them—a small parcel of old-vine Aligoté from a grower on the upper terrace—arrived in bins that had been used the previous day at Vaudren. The entry is in pencil, dated 28 July, and it is the first solid link between the co-op and the affected terrace. Ines closes the notebook and asks Madame Fournier whether she understands why this matters. She does. She understood before Ines arrived.

Wick, a broker, who bought and sold within the same hour on the last crush day and whose refrigerated lorry has been to places his paperwork has not. He operates out of a small office in Beaune with a phone, a laptop, and a reputation for moving fruit faster than anyone else in the region, which is normally an asset and is currently a biosecurity problem. His delivery dockets for the Tarnoux valley are clean—origin declared, variety listed, temperature recorded—but the dockets don't match the grower records at the domaines themselves, because Wick routinely aggregates small lots into single shipments and assigns a new lot number that erases the individual provenance. When Ines reaches him by phone he's cooperative, apologetic, and unable to tell her which grower supplied the grapes that went into any specific delivery because he'd have to reconstruct it from his own notes, which are in a van that is currently in Lyon. The van, he says, will be back tomorrow. Tomorrow is one more day of latency in a trace that's already a week behind the disease. She tells him to call her the moment the van arrives. He promises he will. She believes him and it doesn't help.

A buyer two valleys away took forty cases of Pinot Noir out of the Tarnoux district three weeks ago. He has since sold half of them on to a distributor in Dijon. The buyer is a négociant named Courbet. He is alarmed and helpful. He has already pulled his own delivery records and emailed them to her. But the distributor in Dijon has further split the shipment. He sent it to restaurants, wine shops, and two other négociants. Courbet doesn't have their names. The paperwork breaks apart at each handover, with each lot split. Now, the original forty cases from a single estate have become six smaller shipments. They could be anywhere in Burgundy. The grapes are likely crushed and fermenting by now. But the bins, crates, and pallets were returned to circulation. They may have passed through facilities that handle fruit from clean regions. The trail does not end so much as dissolve. She writes 'OUTWARD – 6 DESTINATIONS – TRACING' in the ledger. She puts a question mark beside it. She knows she may never close this entry.

choices.label: Go and see the grower who refuses.
Hand the outward trail to the neighbouring valley.

nodes.body: The haulier's tachograph is a legal record. It shows exactly where a lorry stood still and for how long. The firm is based in Chalon. It runs three refrigerated trucks that serve the wine valleys from here to the Mâconnais. The tachograph data for the critical period shows stops at seven different estates and the co-op crusher. Unexpectedly, it also shows a stop at a garden centre near Verrière. The lorry was there for forty minutes on a Tuesday afternoon. The garden centre sells potting compost and tomato plants. It has nothing to do with wine. The driver was apparently collecting something for his brother-in-law. This detour means the lorry was parked with its doors open in a place that handles plant material from many suppliers. She adds the garden centre to the watch zone. The manager has never heard of the 2014 order. He has never expected to be regulated under it. He will need a visit, a briefing, and likely some calming down. She will have to find time for that in a day that already has no time in it.

choices.label: Go and see the grower who refuses.
Sit down with the gendarme liaison.
Put the tachograph next to the fair dates.

nodes.body: An unlicensed move: Claude Perrin's tractor and trailer, seen by two neighbours moving along the farm track at dusk with a load of pruned wood. One neighbour, Madame Girard, called it in—she's the anonymous voice on the phone, she admits it when Ines visits her in person—and the other, a retired vigneron named Joubert, confirms he saw the same trailer. Neither of them will testify on paper. Both of them believe Perrin was moving his own prunings from his own rows, which under ordinary circumstances wouldn't matter to anyone, but the circumstances are not ordinary and the pruned wood from an un-surveyed parcel could be carrying the blight to a communal disposal site that has now, retroactively, become a contamination risk. Perrin himself, when she visits his domaine, is standing in his yard with his arms crossed and a look that has already decided she's the enemy. He admits he moved the wood. He says it was his wood, on his land, and he doesn't recognise the authority of a line drawn by someone who's never worked a row in his life. He's partly right. He's also, if the prunings were infected, responsible for the movement of a notifiable organism without a licence. She doesn't know yet which version of the story will survive the month.

choices.label: Go and see the grower who refuses.
Sit down with the gendarme liaison.

nodes.body: The Verrière summer wine fair was held nine days before the first confirmed case. It had a growers' tasting tent and a display of local varieties. There was also a vine-pruning show using cuttings brought in from four different estates. There are no records. The fair was set up by the tourism board and staffed by volunteers. Nobody thought to write down which vines came from where. The cuttings were simply placed in buckets of water on a trestle table. They were labelled by variety, not origin. Several hundred visitors handled them over a Saturday afternoon. If any cuttings came from an infected vineyard, and if any visitor carried bits on their hands or clothes to another estate, then the fair is a single point of failure that nobody can trace. The fair organiser is reached by phone. He is sorry and confused. 'It's just a few branches in a bucket,' he says. She has to explain, gently, that a few branches in a bucket is exactly how this germ moves. He goes quiet. She adds 'FAIR – 9 DAYS PRE – NO RECORDS' to the ledger and underlines it twice.

choices.label: Sit down with the gendarme liaison.

nodes.body: Some paperwork does not match. The same batch of young-vine delivery tags shows up in two growers' records on two different days. This means either the nursery counted a shipment twice, or one grower recorded a delivery that came from the other's holding, not directly from the nursery. The gap is small, just a single pallet of rootlings. But the dates matter. If the rootlings moved between estates after they arrived, that is an unlicensed transfer between holdings during the likely infection window. She spreads both growers' delivery slips side by side on the trestle table. She traces the dates with her finger. The mismatch is clear: the same tag number, different receipt dates, different places. One of these records is wrong. This means one of these growers has moved plant material they should not have. The movement trail the valley relies on has a gap in it. She takes photos of both slips and staples them together. The staple is the closest thing to an official action she can take until she knows which grower's paperwork is the lie.

Cray, compliance officer, arrives from the préfecture with a clipboard and a manner that turns every conversation into a statement. He's young, neat, wearing a tie even in the August heat, and he's been sent to review the movement licences and ensure that the enforcement protocols are being correctly applied. He asks to see the ledger. He reads it carefully, page by page, without comment, and then he asks—looking up, pen poised—whether the entries in the 'what she was told' column are admissible as evidence or merely as notes. She tells him they're notes. He makes a small sound, not quite a sigh, and underlines something on his own clipboard. The room's temperature shifts. She understands, watching him, that his report will determine whether the préfecture backs her decisions or distances itself from them, and that the column she invented for the truth that doesn't fit the form is also the column that will look worst under legal scrutiny. Cray is not her enemy—he's doing his job—but his job is to find the gap between what happened and what's defensible, and she's been creating that gap for days without realising it.

choices.label: Total up the book before going on.
Walk the queue at the hall and listen.

nodes.body: The roadblock at the old bridge, a narrow stone crossing where the D4 drops into the river valley, staffed by two gendarmes who have been told to be firm and not told what to do about the school bus. The bus route runs through the surveillance zone—it has to, there's no other road—and the driver, a woman named Sylvie who's been driving the valley run for fifteen years, is standing beside her bus with the timetable in her hand and fourteen children waiting at the stop on the other side of the barrier. The gendarmes are uncomfortable. Sylvie is polite and insistent. The children are late for school. Ines, arriving to sort out the situation, finds herself facing a choice between the letter of the order and the simple, obvious fact that the valley's ordinary life will not stop for a disease, cannot stop, because children still need to learn and parents still need to work and the bus still needs to run. She tells the gendarmes to let the bus through but to record the plates, the time, and the exact route. They do. Sylvie thanks her. The bus moves on, and Ines knows she's just created a precedent she'll have to explain to Cray. She writes 'SCHOOL BUS – PASS – RECORDED' in the ledger and puts an asterisk beside it, meaning: this one will come back.

choices.label: Total up the book before going on.
Walk the queue at the hall and listen.
Go back to Vaudren and open the gate with him.

nodes.body: The prosecution question: whether to build a file on the Perrin unlicensed movement now, which will end the cooperation she is currently living on. Perrin is well-known in the valley, his family has been here for generations, and if she initiates a formal enforcement action—even a warning letter—the news will travel faster than any official notification. The growers who are currently phoning her with information, who are bringing her their spray diaries and their delivery dockets, will stop. They'll stop because they'll see a neighbour being prosecuted for moving his own prunings and they'll decide the safest thing is to tell her nothing. She knows this. Cray, who has no history with the valley, does not know it, or does not care, and he's watching her across the trestle table with the ledger open at the Perrin entry and his pen hovering over his own notes. He asks what she intends to do. She tells him she's still considering. He writes something down. The moment stretches. She's been in the job long enough to know that the right enforcement action at the wrong time is worse than no enforcement action at all, but she can't say that out loud without sounding like she's choosing loyalty over law. She might be.

choices.label: Walk the queue at the hall and listen.
Go back to Vaudren and open the gate with him.
Read what the papers are printing.

nodes.body: The disinfectant station at the valley mouth, where the footbaths—plastic trays filled with a quaternary ammonium solution—have gone sour and nobody has changed the drum in three days. The trays were set up on the first morning by a volunteer from the village, who meant well and then went back to his job at the post office and assumed someone else would maintain them. The solution is cloudy, the concentration unknown, and every vehicle that has crossed the zone boundary in the last seventy-two hours has driven through a disinfectant that was doing nothing. She finds the trays herself, on a routine drive round, and stands looking at them for a full minute. The failure is precisely the kind of gap Cray is looking for—a biosecurity measure that existed on paper and not in practice—and it will appear in his report regardless of who she blames. She photographs the trays, the drum, the date on the delivery docket, and then she changes the solution herself, kneeling on the verge in her field trousers, because there is no one else to do it and it needs doing now. A car slows down. The driver watches her through the windscreen and then moves on. She adds 'DISINFECTANT FAILURE – 72 HRS' to the ledger, in the margin, in her smallest writing, as though making it smaller will make it less significant.

choices.label: Go back to Vaudren and open the gate with him.
Read what the papers are printing.

nodes.body: A grower who will not comply: Alain Fauvet, standing in his own gateway on the Montjoie slope, arms crossed, with his mother Céline behind him and the old-vine Grenache stretching down the hill beyond. He says the line is drawn wrong—that the containment zone boundary cuts through the middle of his property, that the bottom three rows are inside and the top six are outside, and that the distinction is meaningless because the soil is the same soil and the vines are the same vines and the blight does not stop at a wax-pencil mark on a ten-year-old map. He's right about the line. The map is old and the boundary was drawn from a desk in the village hall using a ruler and a photocopied cadastral plan that hasn't been updated since the new plantings went in. The line is arbitrary because all lines are arbitrary when you're drawing them on a map rather than walking the ground. He's wrong about what follows, though, because being right about the line doesn't change the fact that the line exists and she's legally required to enforce it. She tells him this. He doesn't move from the gateway. His mother, behind him, says nothing, and her silence is heavier than anything Alain could say. Ines stands in the track with the afternoon sun on her neck and feels the weight of an order that is correct on paper and impossible on the ground, and she doesn't yet know how she's going to resolve this without either losing the Fauvet family entirely or proving Alain's point about the arbitrariness of lines.

choices.label: Read what the papers are printing.

nodes.body: Sergeant Lefèvre, the gendarmerie liaison, wants to know exactly which of her instructions are law and which are advice. He's sitting in the hall with his notebook open, a careful, methodical man who has been given an assignment he didn't ask for and who is trying to do it correctly. The public-order powers are clear, he says: he can enforce a road closure, a movement ban, an exclusion from premises. But the hygiene advice—the footbaths, the vehicle washing, the request that growers wear dedicated clothing in affected rows—those are recommendations, not regulations, and he can't order a constable to enforce a recommendation. He needs her to tell him, specifically, which measures carry legal force and which carry only her authority as district officer. She starts listing them, and as she does she realises the second list—the advice, the requests, the 'we strongly recommend'—is much the longer of the two. Most of what she's been doing all week, most of what she's asked people to do, has no legal backing at all. It's been working because the valley chose to cooperate. Lefèvre writes it all down, impassive, and when he's finished he closes his notebook and looks at her. 'I need this in writing,' he says. 'Before Monday.' She nods. The ledger is full of things she needs to put in writing before Monday.

choices.label: Total up the book before going on.
Separate the law from the advice.

nodes.body: The second week begins with a heavy dew, which settles on every leaf in the valley and sits there, glinting, as the sun comes up. Everybody says it's good—good for slowing the spread, good for keeping the inoculum down—and nobody can say why they believe this. It's probably folk knowledge, probably wrong, and she doesn't correct it because the belief is doing more for morale than any official briefing. The dew also means the vines are heavy with moisture, which makes the rows harder to survey but easier to sample, and the lab in Colmar has asked for fresh tissue before the heat of the afternoon. She collects the samples herself, walking the affected rows at Vaudren in the early light, and the quiet of the valley at dawn is almost peaceful—almost enough to make her forget for a moment why she's here. Then she sees the next canker, small and fresh on a cordon she inspected three days ago, and the quiet stops being peaceful.

The second week in the ledger: fifty-three licences granted, twenty-one refused, and four she is no longer sure about. The four are entries from the first three days. She made them quickly, under pressure, with incomplete information. She approved a movement of empty bins on a verbal assurance. She granted a derogation for a grower who needed to cross the line for a family medical appointment. She made a decision about shared equipment that seemed sensible at the time and now reads as reckless. She re-reads them at the trestle table, the ledger open at the early pages. The woman who wrote those entries is not the same woman reading them now, ten days deeper into the outbreak with everything she has learned since. The entries are defensible, probably. They are also the ones Cray will focus on if his review turns adversarial. She puts an asterisk beside each of them. It is the same mark she used for the school bus. The marks are accumulating now. They form a constellation of decisions that seemed vital at the time and look, in hindsight, like a pattern she did not see herself creating.

choices.label: Be there for the removal team.

nodes.body: The second week in the valley: the queue at the hall is shorter and quieter, which is somehow worse. The people who still come are not the ones seeking licences but the ones who have nowhere else to go—a grower's wife with a question about the school exemption, a retired vigneron offering to help with the footbaths, a young man who just wants to sit in the hall for an hour because his own house is inside the zone and the silence there is getting to him. The queue has changed shape, become something else, a kind of informal support group that meets around the coffee urn and trades information the official channels don't carry. Ines realises, watching them, that the queue was never about the paperwork—it was about being told something by someone with a name, someone who would look at them and acknowledge that their problem was real. The people who've stopped coming are the ones who've given up believing she can help them. The ones who remain are the ones who still trust her, or who have no one else to trust. She doesn't know which group worries her more.

The second week at Vaudren: the affected rows stripped, the vines pulled and the rootstock grubbed out, the soil treated and the trellis wires cut down, and Paul Rennick still coming out to open the gate. He does it every morning, as though nothing has changed, as though his domaine is still a working vineyard and not a quarantine site with bare earth where his best Chardonnay used to be. He walks her through the cleared rows with a quiet dignity that's harder to witness than any anger would be. He points out where the new trellising will go, when the time comes, and he asks her, without quite asking, whether the soil will be safe to replant. She tells him the lab results aren't back yet. He nods. He's been nodding at her answers for ten days now, accepting each one even when it tells him nothing, and she's starting to understand that his politeness is a form of endurance—that he's surviving the standstill by being civil, one interaction at a time, and that the day he stops opening the gate is the day something fundamental breaks. She walks the bare rows with him, matching his pace, and tries to be worthy of the gate.

choices.label: Hear the case for the heritage clone.

nodes.body: The second week in the press: a photograph of a vine-pulling in the Languedoc, not in this region, running above a story about the Tarnoux outbreak that quotes an unnamed source at the ministry saying the containment measures are 'under review.' The photograph shows a mechanical digger uprooting old vines in a cloud of dust, and it's dramatic and misleading and exactly the image the tourism board has been dreading. The local correspondent, a man named Dev Antrobus who's been accurate so far, has filed three stories this week and is working on a fourth, and his questions are getting sharper. The préfecture's press office wants Ines to give a statement, on camera—something reassuring, something that emphasises the containment is working. She reads the draft they've sent her and it's full of language she would never use in the hall, in the queue, in front of people whose livelihoods the words are meant to protect. She deletes half of it and writes her own draft, shorter, blunter, and sends it back. They will probably rewrite it again. She goes outside to the lay-by and finds Antrobus already there, camera ready, asking the question she's been avoiding: whether anyone has calculated the total economic loss. She hasn't. She doesn't want to. The number will be the lede of his next story, whether she gives it to him or not.

The second week at home: her own kitchen at one in the morning, boots on newspaper by the door, the cat winding around her ankles and the kettle just boiled and the silence of her own house pressing in on her like something physical. She hasn't been here for more than an hour in four days. The mail is stacked on the table, the plants on the windowsill are dead, and the light on the answering machine is blinking with messages she hasn't listened to. She sits at the kitchen table with a cup of tea and doesn't drink it, just holds it, feeling the warmth through the ceramic, and for twenty minutes she is not the district officer, not the keeper of the ledger, not the face that appears at the hall door every morning. She's just a person in a kitchen, exhausted, with boots that smell of vineyard soil and a phone that will ring again in three hours. She thinks about the Fauvet family on the slope, about Rennick opening his gate, about Sarre's polytunnel, and she writes nothing down. These twenty minutes are not in the ledger. They're the only thing today that hasn't been.

choices.label: Go up to the refusal at Montjoie.

nodes.body: The valuation: a valuer sent from the ministry's compensation office, a grower, and a number that must stand up in eighteen months when somebody appeals it. The valuer is a middle-aged man named Moreau who has done this before. He has mostly done livestock valuations and crop losses. He is walking the cleared rows at Vaudren with a clipboard and a quiet, professional manner that is somehow more intrusive than any official inspection. He asks Rennick about the yield history, the market price, and the cost of replanting. Rennick answers in a flat voice. It is nothing like the voice he uses when he opens the gate. The number Moreau writes down will decide what the ministry pays for the lost vines. The gap between what the vines were worth on paper and what they were worth to Rennick—sixty years of his family's work, the rootstock his grandfather selected, the clones that produce the particular Vaudren Chardonnay—cannot be expressed in a currency the scheme can handle. Moreau knows this, she can tell, and he writes the number anyway. His job is to produce a figure that will survive an audit. It is not a figure that is fair. It is a figure that is defensible. She watches him work and adds nothing to the ledger. The ledger was not designed for the gap between a spreadsheet and a family.

The removal team, competent, unhurried, and unbearable to watch, working through the affected rows at Vaudren in an order they will not deviate from. They're a crew of four, with a tracked digger and a chipper, contracted by the ministry from a company that specialises in agricultural clearance, and they've done this before—more times than anyone in the valley wants to think about—but not here, not in the Tarnoux, not on vines that someone's grandfather planted. They work methodically, one vine at a time, and the sound of the chipper is the dominant noise in the valley for the whole morning. Rennick doesn't watch. He stays in his office with the door closed, and when she knocks after the crew have finished the first row, he doesn't answer. She lets him be. She stands at the edge of the terrace and watches the digger lift the next vine, its rootball coming up with a wet tearing sound, and she thinks about the ledger entry she will write for this—'REMOVAL – VAUDREN – ROWS 4-11'—and how inadequate the words will be. The crew foreman asks if they should stop for lunch. She tells them to keep going. There's no good way to stop.

nodes.body: Burial or incineration: a water table that runs close to the surface here, a licence from the environment agency, a wind direction that will carry the smoke across the village if they burn, and a commune that will remember the choice for years after the disease is forgotten. The pruned wood, the pulled vines, the contaminated trellis stakes and irrigation pipe—all of it must be destroyed under biosecure conditions. The two options are an engineered pit with an impermeable liner, or a controlled burn on a day when the wind blows away from the houses. The pit is slow, costly, and safe. The burn is fast, visible, and alarming to anyone who sees the smoke. The mayor has been cooperative so far, but she is adamant about the burn. The village will panic, she says, if they see a pyre on the Vaudren terrace. The environment agency wants the burial because the soil here is thin and the pit will not reach the groundwater if it is lined properly. Ines sits in the hall with both sets of paperwork and a phone that will not stop ringing. She tries to decide which future resentment she is willing to live with. She writes 'DISPOSAL METHOD – PENDING' in the ledger. The word 'pending' is starting to feel like her signature.

nodes.body: The Vaudren heritage clone is a selection of Chardonnay that exists nowhere else. It is sixty years of massal selection by Rennick's grandfather. Vines were chosen from the best rows, propagated on site, and never commercialised. The clone produces the distinctive mineral note that the négociants describe as 'Vaudren typicity.' Rennick, in the quiet of his office after the removal team has gone, asks whether there is any chance of saving the propagation wood. The vines themselves are destroyed, but the clone lives in the grafted cuttings taken for the nursery block three months ago. Those cuttings are now sitting in pots at Les Sources, inside the containment zone, unable to be moved. He wants an exemption to keep the genetic material in a secure facility. It is a good argument: the clone is unique and irreplaceable. If it is lost, the Vaudren style is lost with it. It is also exactly the kind of special pleading that the regulations are designed to prevent. If she grants an exemption for the Vaudren clone, every other grower in the valley with a 'heritage' vine will expect the same. The precedent will be quoted back at her for the rest of the outbreak. Rennick looks at her across his desk with the same expression he wore when he opened the gate. He is a man asking for something reasonable, in a situation where reason is not the standard. She tells him she will consider it. He nods. The gate, this time, is the one he has opened in her.

nodes.body: The contiguous removal argument: take out the neighbouring terraces on suspicion alone—the vines immediately adjacent to the affected rows, plus the parcels that share a trellis line or an irrigation run—as a pre-emptive measure to stop the spread. The ministry is pushing for it. The science is ambiguous. The growers whose vines would be pulled are the Fauvet family on the Montjoie slope, the Brayne trellises on the lower terraces, and a small parcel of old-vine Aligoté belonging to a retired couple who have already said they won't survive the loss. If she signs the order, the valley loses three more families' livelihoods in exchange for a reduction in risk that no one can quantify, because nobody knows how the blight moves. If she refuses, and the blight spreads to those terraces anyway, she's the one who chose sentiment over science. The room is very quiet. Karine, who has been through this in Switzerland, is watching her from the other side of the table with an expression that says: I can't tell you what to do but I know what I did. Ines picks up the pen. She doesn't write yet. She's trying to feel her way to the version of this decision she can live with in a year, or five years, or on the morning she opens a ledger from a different valley and sees the same choice staring back at her from a different page.

A refusal: Alain Fauvet standing in his own gateway, his mother Céline behind him, and the old-vine Grenache stretching down the slope with the afternoon light on it, and no version of the next hour that anybody wants. She's come to tell him formally that his parcel is subject to a pre-emptive removal order, and he knows it, he's known since he saw the ministry car coming up the track. He doesn't raise his voice. He stands in the gateway and tells her, very quietly, that his mother planted some of these vines with her own hands in 1973, that the Grenache has survived three heatwaves and two freezes and the phylloxera that took the lower terrace in the 1980s, and that he will not watch a ministry digger uproot it on suspicion alone. He says the word 'suspicion' the way someone might say 'rumour.' She tells him she hasn't signed the order yet. He says he knows that too, and that's why he's still talking to her. The sun is moving behind the ridge and the temperature is dropping and his mother, behind him, still hasn't spoken. Ines has been standing in this gateway for ten minutes and it feels like an hour, and she's trying to find the sentence that will let her leave without either lying to him or destroying something she can't rebuild. The sentence doesn't exist. She writes nothing in the ledger tonight, because the thing she would have to write is not ready to be written.

The Colmar laboratory result comes in as a table rather than an answer. It has columns of accession numbers, primer sets, Ct values, and a confidence interval that needs a statistician to interpret. She reads it twice. The first time she scans for the bottom line. The second time she reads the methodology notes. What she finds is that the organism is definitely the notifiable vascular pathogen they suspected. It is definitely present in the Vaudren samples. It is definitely not a strain they have seen before in France. The table also shows, in a footnote that is easy to miss, that the nearest genetic match is a strain from a vineyard in northern Italy. It was reported two years ago but never fully traced. The distance between the Italian outbreak and the Tarnoux valley is about four hundred kilometres. That is too far for wind dispersal and too far for insect vectors. It suggests, very quietly, that the introduction came in on imported plant material. Somewhere in the valley's nursery records, in the delivery dockets and the broker's paperwork and the co-op's informal notebook, there is a shipment that connects an Italian vine to a French terrace. The table from Colmar does not identify it. It just tells her where to look. She closes the email and opens the ledger. For the first time in twelve days, she knows what question she is trying to answer.

Serology on the Montjoie Grenache: ELISA is positive. Antibody is present, but the vines show no clinical signs. No cankers, no discolouration, no wilt. The result means either an old, resolved exposure, or a recent, silent infection that is still incubating. In the first case, the vines met the organism and beat it, which would be remarkable and worth studying. In the second, the vines met the organism and it is spreading through the vascular system right now, invisibly, while the Fauvet family trim their canopy and wait for her to say their vines are safe. She cannot tell the difference without a PCR confirmation. The PCR will take another five days. In those five days, the pre-emptive removal order sits on her desk like an unexploded device. She phones the Colmar lab and asks them to prioritise the Montjoie samples. The technician who answers tells her, politely, that everyone asks for prioritisation. She thanks him and hangs up. She writes 'MONTJOIE – POSITIVE SEROLOGY – NO CLINICAL SIGNS – AWAITING PCR' in the ledger. The entry is the length of a sentence and the weight of several families.

nodes.body: A negative that is not conclusive, on a parcel of young vines at the Brayne trellises. Lucie Brayne's scout found two suspect marks there last week. The PCR came back negative. But the sampling protocol only tested three vines, the lesions were small, and the pathologist's note says 'cannot exclude early infection due to limited sample.' It is the most frustrating result possible. The science says, technically, 'not detected.' The caveat says, in effect, 'but don't rely on it.' Lucie Brayne is waiting by her phone for the news. If she hears 'negative,' she will assume her trellises are clear, her pickers can come back, and her harvest might still be saved. But the caveat, the small print about sample size and lesion age, matters. The negative is not a clean bill of health. It is a photograph of one moment taken with a poor lens. Ines must decide whether to tell Lucie the good news, that the test was negative, or the complicated news, that the negative might not mean anything. The decision matters because Lucie's next choices depend on what she believes. She will decide whether to start picking and whether to open her gates. Ines writes 'BRAYNE – NEGATIVE (LIMITED SAMPLE) – NOTIFY WITH CAVEAT' in the ledger. Then she picks up the phone and makes the call. She chooses each word carefully. She knows she is about to deliver both relief and doubt in the same sentence, and only one of them will be heard.
